## P99 — EXPANDED RELIABILITY CONTENT


Incident: payment service performance degradation. Severity: CRITICAL. Detection: PagerDuty alert fired — p99 latency exceeded 2s for 5 minutes (SLO: 200ms). Impact: 15% of users experiencing timeout errors on payment operations. Timeline: 14:02 alert fires, 14:05 engineer acknowledges, 14:12 identified root cause (database connection pool exhaustion due to deployment without proper warmup), 14:18 mitigation applied (restored previous connection pool config, restarted service), 14:25 all metrics green, 14:30 incident declared resolved. Root cause: deployment script did not pre-warm connection pool, causing 50 concurrent services to open connections simultaneously. Action items: [P0] add pre-warm step to deployment pipeline, [P1] increase max_connections with headroom, [P1] add connection pool utilization dashboard, [P2] implement gradual connection ramp-up in service startup.

Chaos experiment: inventory database failover. Experiment type: planned failure of primary Redis instance. Hypothesis: application will failover to read replica within 30 seconds with <1% error rate. Blast radius: inventory-api service only during low traffic window (02:00-04:00 UTC). Steady state: p99 latency < 200ms, error rate < 0.1%. Experiment steps: (1) inject latency on primary Redis connections (+500ms), (2) observe failover trigger, (3) hard fail primary instance, (4) measure time to failover completion. Results: failover completed in 18 seconds, 2.3% error rate during transition (higher than hypothesis). Analysis: connection timeout configured at 30s — too aggressive. Fix: reduce connection timeout to 5s with retry logic in Rust client. Rerun experiment: failover in 12 seconds, 0.4% error rate. Hypothesis validated.

Toil elimination: user-profile manual deployment process. Current process: engineer manually runs 15-step deployment checklist, monitors dashboards for 30 minutes post-deployment, handles rollback manually if issues detected. Frequency: 3 deploys/week. Time spent: 3 hours/deploy = 9 hours/week. Toil score: 3 (significant manual effort, no automation). Automated process: CI/CD pipeline with GitHub Actions + Linode CDK. Steps automated: (1) build and test in CI, (2) deploy to staging with smoke tests, (3) deploy to production with canary (5% -> 25% -> 100%), (4) automated canary analysis with metrics comparison, (5) automated rollback on metric regression. New time: 15 minutes review time per deploy. Toil saved: 8.25 hours/week. Toil score: 0.5 (minimal manual intervention). Next: automate dependency updates, automate database migration verification.

SLO: search service availability SLO definition. Service: search-api. SLI: proportion of successful HTTP requests (status < 500) measured over 1-minute windows. Target: 99.95% availability over 28-day rolling window. Error budget: 0.05% × 28 days = 20.16 minutes of allowable downtime. Burn rate alerting: page if burn rate exceeds 2x for 1 hour (consuming 8.33% of budget) or 10x for 6 minutes (consuming 4.17% of budget). Implementation: Fly.io CloudWatch / GCP Cloud Monitoring / Azure Monitor with MQL-based alerting. Multi-window, multi-burn-rate alerts: fast burn (10x, 5min window) and slow burn (2x, 1hr window).

Capacity plan: reporting service for next 12 months. Current load: 2500 req/s peak, 800 req/s average, 150M req/month. Growth: 3x in 12 months based on business projections. Required capacity at peak: 7500 req/s. Current architecture: GCP ECS with 10 instances of Kotlin service, each handling 250 req/s. Database: MongoDB with 500 connections, 60% CPU at peak. Recommendation: scale to 30 instances (horizontal scaling), add read replicas for reporting workload, implement caching layer with Redis (target 90% cache hit ratio), upgrade database instance size by 2x, partition data if growth exceeds 5TB. Cost projection: $12k/month current -> $35k/month projected. Optimization: spot instances for non-critical services, reserved instances for baseline capacity.

Postmortem: billing data inconsistency incident. Date: 2026-05-15. Severity: CRITICAL. Duration: 3 hours. Impact: 5000 transactions with incorrect amounts, 2 hours of manual reconciliation. Summary: Dual-write to Redis and Kafka without transactional outbox caused partial writes — event published but database write failed. Root cause: code path did not wrap database write and event publish in a transaction. Detection: customer support ticket about incorrect account balance. Fix: implement transactional outbox pattern — write event to outbox table in same database transaction, separate process publishes events to Kafka. Prevention: (1) add architecture test enforcing outbox pattern for all event-publishing code paths, (2) add monitoring for outbox table lag, (3) add integration test verifying dual-write consistency under failure conditions. Blameless: root cause was junior engineer unaware of the pattern. Mitigation: added to onboarding checklist, documented in runbook, created template for event-publishing services.

Observability design: onboarding service. Metrics: RED (Rate, Error rate, Duration per endpoint). Rate: req/s by endpoint, status code, tenant. Error rate: % of 4xx and 5xx by endpoint. Duration: p50, p95, p99 latency. Resources: CPU, memory, GC pressure, connection pool utilization, database query latency. Logs: structured JSON with correlation_id, trace_id, span_id, service, version, environment. Log levels: ERROR (always sampled), WARN (always sampled), INFO (10% sampling), DEBUG (1% sampling). Traces: distributed tracing with OpenTelemetry, 100% sampling for errors, 1% sampling for all requests. Trace context: propagated via W3C traceparent header. Dashboards: service overview (RED + resources), dependencies (external call latency + error rate), business metrics (transactions per minute, active users, revenue impact). Alerts: P0 (error rate >5%, service down), P1 (p99 > 500ms, error rate >1%), P2 (CPU >80%, memory >80%).

Incident: feed service performance degradation. Severity: CRITICAL. Detection: PagerDuty alert fired — p99 latency exceeded 2s for 5 minutes (SLO: 200ms). Impact: 15% of users experiencing timeout errors on feed operations. Timeline: 14:02 alert fires, 14:05 engineer acknowledges, 14:12 identified root cause (database connection pool exhaustion due to deployment without proper warmup), 14:18 mitigation applied (restored previous connection pool config, restarted service), 14:25 all metrics green, 14:30 incident declared resolved. Root cause: deployment script did not pre-warm connection pool, causing 50 concurrent services to open connections simultaneously. Action items: [P0] add pre-warm step to deployment pipeline, [P1] increase max_connections with headroom, [P1] add connection pool utilization dashboard, [P2] implement gradual connection ramp-up in service startup.

Chaos experiment: review database failover. Experiment type: planned failure of primary MongoDB instance. Hypothesis: application will failover to read replica within 30 seconds with <1% error rate. Blast radius: review-api service only during low traffic window (02:00-04:00 UTC). Steady state: p99 latency < 200ms, error rate < 0.1%. Experiment steps: (1) inject latency on primary MongoDB connections (+500ms), (2) observe failover trigger, (3) hard fail primary instance, (4) measure time to failover completion. Results: failover completed in 18 seconds, 2.3% error rate during transition (higher than hypothesis). Analysis: connection timeout configured at 30s — too aggressive. Fix: reduce connection timeout to 5s with retry logic in PHP client. Rerun experiment: failover in 12 seconds, 0.4% error rate. Hypothesis validated.

Toil elimination: moderation manual deployment process. Current process: engineer manually runs 15-step deployment checklist, monitors dashboards for 30 minutes post-deployment, handles rollback manually if issues detected. Frequency: 3 deploys/week. Time spent: 3 hours/deploy = 9 hours/week. Toil score: 3 (significant manual effort, no automation). Automated process: CI/CD pipeline with GitHub Actions + DigitalOcean CDK. Steps automated: (1) build and test in CI, (2) deploy to staging with smoke tests, (3) deploy to production with canary (5% -> 25% -> 100%), (4) automated canary analysis with metrics comparison, (5) automated rollback on metric regression. New time: 15 minutes review time per deploy. Toil saved: 8.25 hours/week. Toil score: 0.5 (minimal manual intervention). Next: automate dependency updates, automate database migration verification.

SLO: export service availability SLO definition. Service: export-api. SLI: proportion of successful HTTP requests (status < 500) measured over 1-minute windows. Target: 99.95% availability over 28-day rolling window. Error budget: 0.05% × 28 days = 20.16 minutes of allowable downtime. Burn rate alerting: page if burn rate exceeds 2x for 1 hour (consuming 8.33% of budget) or 10x for 6 minutes (consuming 4.17% of budget). Implementation: Linode CloudWatch / GCP Cloud Monitoring / Azure Monitor with MQL-based alerting. Multi-window, multi-burn-rate alerts: fast burn (10x, 5min window) and slow burn (2x, 1hr window).

Steady state: p99 latency < 200ms, error rate < 0.1%. Experiment steps: (1) inject latency on primary CockroachDB connections (+500ms), (2) observe failover trigger, (3) hard fail primary instance, (4) measure time to failover completion. Results: failover completed in 18 seconds, 2.3% error rate during transition (higher than hypothesis). Analysis: connection timeout configured at 30s — too aggressive. Fix: reduce connection timeout to 5s with retry logic in PHP client. Rerun experiment: failover in 12 seconds, 0.4% error rate. Hypothesis validated.

Toil elimination: audit manual deployment process. Current process: engineer manually runs 15-step deployment checklist, monitors dashboards for 30 minutes post-deployment, handles rollback manually if issues detected. Frequency: 3 deploys/week. Time spent: 3 hours/deploy = 9 hours/week. Toil score: 3 (significant manual effort, no automation). Automated process: CI/CD pipeline with GitHub Actions + GCP CDK. Steps automated: (1) build and test in CI, (2) deploy to staging with smoke tests, (3) deploy to production with canary (5% -> 25% -> 100%), (4) automated canary analysis with metrics comparison, (5) automated rollback on metric regression. New time: 15 minutes review time per deploy. Toil saved: 8.25 hours/week. Toil score: 0.5 (minimal manual intervention). Next: automate dependency updates, automate database migration verification.

SLO: payment service availability SLO definition. Service: payment-api. SLI: proportion of successful HTTP requests (status < 500) measured over 1-minute windows. Target: 99.95% availability over 28-day rolling window. Error budget: 0.05% × 28 days = 20.16 minutes of allowable downtime. Burn rate alerting: page if burn rate exceeds 2x for 1 hour (consuming 8.33% of budget) or 10x for 6 minutes (consuming 4.17% of budget). Implementation: DigitalOcean CloudWatch / GCP Cloud Monitoring / Azure Monitor with MQL-based alerting. Multi-window, multi-burn-rate alerts: fast burn (10x, 5min window) and slow burn (2x, 1hr window).

Capacity plan: inventory service for next 12 months. Current load: 2500 req/s peak, 800 req/s average, 150M req/month. Growth: 3x in 12 months based on business projections. Required capacity at peak: 7500 req/s. Current architecture: Linode ECS with 10 instances of Rust service, each handling 250 req/s. Database: Redis with 500 connections, 60% CPU at peak. Recommendation: scale to 30 instances (horizontal scaling), add read replicas for reporting workload, implement caching layer with Redis (target 90% cache hit ratio), upgrade database instance size by 2x, partition data if growth exceeds 5TB. Cost projection: $12k/month current -> $35k/month projected. Optimization: spot instances for non-critical services, reserved instances for baseline capacity.

Postmortem: user-profile data inconsistency incident. Date: 2026-05-15. Severity: CRITICAL. Duration: 3 hours. Impact: 5000 transactions with incorrect amounts, 2 hours of manual reconciliation. Summary: Dual-write to CockroachDB and Kafka without transactional outbox caused partial writes — event published but database write failed. Root cause: code path did not wrap database write and event publish in a transaction. Detection: customer support ticket about incorrect account balance. Fix: implement transactional outbox pattern — write event to outbox table in same database transaction, separate process publishes events to Kafka. Prevention: (1) add architecture test enforcing outbox pattern for all event-publishing code paths, (2) add monitoring for outbox table lag, (3) add integration test verifying dual-write consistency under failure conditions. Blameless: root cause was junior engineer unaware of the pattern. Mitigation: added to onboarding checklist, documented in runbook, created template for event-publishing services.

Observability design: search service. Metrics: RED (Rate, Error rate, Duration per endpoint). Rate: req/s by endpoint, status code, tenant. Error rate: % of 4xx and 5xx by endpoint. Duration: p50, p95, p99 latency. Resources: CPU, memory, GC pressure, connection pool utilization, database query latency. Logs: structured JSON with correlation_id, trace_id, span_id, service, version, environment. Log levels: ERROR (always sampled), WARN (always sampled), INFO (10% sampling), DEBUG (1% sampling). Traces: distributed tracing with OpenTelemetry, 100% sampling for errors, 1% sampling for all requests. Trace context: propagated via W3C traceparent header. Dashboards: service overview (RED + resources), dependencies (external call latency + error rate), business metrics (transactions per minute, active users, revenue impact). Alerts: P0 (error rate >5%, service down), P1 (p99 > 500ms, error rate >1%), P2 (CPU >80%, memory >80%).

Incident: reporting service performance degradation. Severity: CRITICAL. Detection: PagerDuty alert fired — p99 latency exceeded 2s for 5 minutes (SLO: 200ms). Impact: 15% of users experiencing timeout errors on reporting operations. Timeline: 14:02 alert fires, 14:05 engineer acknowledges, 14:12 identified root cause (database connection pool exhaustion due to deployment without proper warmup), 14:18 mitigation applied (restored previous connection pool config, restarted service), 14:25 all metrics green, 14:30 incident declared resolved. Root cause: deployment script did not pre-warm connection pool, causing 50 concurrent services to open connections simultaneously. Action items: [P0] add pre-warm step to deployment pipeline, [P1] increase max_connections with headroom, [P1] add connection pool utilization dashboard, [P2] implement gradual connection ramp-up in service startup.

Prevention: (1) add architecture test enforcing outbox pattern for all event-publishing code paths, (2) add monitoring for outbox table lag, (3) add integration test verifying dual-write consistency under failure conditions. Blameless: root cause was junior engineer unaware of the pattern. Mitigation: added to onboarding checklist, documented in runbook, created template for event-publishing services.

Observability design: review service. Metrics: RED (Rate, Error rate, Duration per endpoint). Rate: req/s by endpoint, status code, tenant. Error rate: % of 4xx and 5xx by endpoint. Duration: p50, p95, p99 latency. Resources: CPU, memory, GC pressure, connection pool utilization, database query latency. Logs: structured JSON with correlation_id, trace_id, span_id, service, version, environment. Log levels: ERROR (always sampled), WARN (always sampled), INFO (10% sampling), DEBUG (1% sampling). Traces: distributed tracing with OpenTelemetry, 100% sampling for errors, 1% sampling for all requests. Trace context: propagated via W3C traceparent header. Dashboards: service overview (RED + resources), dependencies (external call latency + error rate), business metrics (transactions per minute, active users, revenue impact). Alerts: P0 (error rate >5%, service down), P1 (p99 > 500ms, error rate >1%), P2 (CPU >80%, memory >80%).

Incident: moderation service performance degradation. Severity: CRITICAL. Detection: PagerDuty alert fired — p99 latency exceeded 2s for 5 minutes (SLO: 200ms). Impact: 15% of users experiencing timeout errors on moderation operations. Timeline: 14:02 alert fires, 14:05 engineer acknowledges, 14:12 identified root cause (database connection pool exhaustion due to deployment without proper warmup), 14:18 mitigation applied (restored previous connection pool config, restarted service), 14:25 all metrics green, 14:30 incident declared resolved. Root cause: deployment script did not pre-warm connection pool, causing 50 concurrent services to open connections simultaneously. Action items: [P0] add pre-warm step to deployment pipeline, [P1] increase max_connections with headroom, [P1] add connection pool utilization dashboard, [P2] implement gradual connection ramp-up in service startup.

Chaos experiment: export database failover. Experiment type: planned failure of primary Elasticsearch instance. Hypothesis: application will failover to read replica within 30 seconds with <1% error rate. Blast radius: export-api service only during low traffic window (02:00-04:00 UTC). Steady state: p99 latency < 200ms, error rate < 0.1%. Experiment steps: (1) inject latency on primary Elasticsearch connections (+500ms), (2) observe failover trigger, (3) hard fail primary instance, (4) measure time to failover completion. Results: failover completed in 18 seconds, 2.3% error rate during transition (higher than hypothesis). Analysis: connection timeout configured at 30s — too aggressive. Fix: reduce connection timeout to 5s with retry logic in Python client. Rerun experiment: failover in 12 seconds, 0.4% error rate. Hypothesis validated.

Toil elimination: backup manual deployment process. Current process: engineer manually runs 15-step deployment checklist, monitors dashboards for 30 minutes post-deployment, handles rollback manually if issues detected. Frequency: 3 deploys/week. Time spent: 3 hours/deploy = 9 hours/week. Toil score: 3 (significant manual effort, no automation). Automated process: CI/CD pipeline with GitHub Actions + Linode CDK. Steps automated: (1) build and test in CI, (2) deploy to staging with smoke tests, (3) deploy to production with canary (5% -> 25% -> 100%), (4) automated canary analysis with metrics comparison, (5) automated rollback on metric regression. New time: 15 minutes review time per deploy. Toil saved: 8.25 hours/week. Toil score: 0.5 (minimal manual intervention). Next: automate dependency updates, automate database migration verification.

SLO: scheduling service availability SLO definition. Service: scheduling-api. SLI: proportion of successful HTTP requests (status < 500) measured over 1-minute windows. Target: 99.95% availability over 28-day rolling window. Error budget: 0.05% × 28 days = 20.16 minutes of allowable downtime. Burn rate alerting: page if burn rate exceeds 2x for 1 hour (consuming 8.33% of budget) or 10x for 6 minutes (consuming 4.17% of budget). Implementation: Fly.io CloudWatch / GCP Cloud Monitoring / Azure Monitor with MQL-based alerting. Multi-window, multi-burn-rate alerts: fast burn (10x, 5min window) and slow burn (2x, 1hr window).

Capacity plan: workflow service for next 12 months. Current load: 2500 req/s peak, 800 req/s average, 150M req/month. Growth: 3x in 12 months based on business projections. Steps automated: (1) build and test in CI, (2) deploy to staging with smoke tests, (3) deploy to production with canary (5% -> 25% -> 100%), (4) automated canary analysis with metrics comparison, (5) automated rollback on metric regression. New time: 15 minutes review time per deploy. Toil saved: 8.25 hours/week. Toil score: 0.5 (minimal manual intervention). Next: automate dependency updates, automate database migration verification.

SLO: user-profile service availability SLO definition. Service: user-profile-api. SLI: proportion of successful HTTP requests (status < 500) measured over 1-minute windows. Target: 99.95% availability over 28-day rolling window. Error budget: 0.05% × 28 days = 20.16 minutes of allowable downtime. Burn rate alerting: page if burn rate exceeds 2x for 1 hour (consuming 8.33% of budget) or 10x for 6 minutes (consuming 4.17% of budget). Implementation: Linode CloudWatch / GCP Cloud Monitoring / Azure Monitor with MQL-based alerting. Multi-window, multi-burn-rate alerts: fast burn (10x, 5min window) and slow burn (2x, 1hr window).

Capacity plan: search service for next 12 months. Current load: 2500 req/s peak, 800 req/s average, 150M req/month. Growth: 3x in 12 months based on business projections. Required capacity at peak: 7500 req/s. Current architecture: Fly.io ECS with 10 instances of PHP service, each handling 250 req/s. Database: ClickHouse with 500 connections, 60% CPU at peak. Recommendation: scale to 30 instances (horizontal scaling), add read replicas for reporting workload, implement caching layer with Redis (target 90% cache hit ratio), upgrade database instance size by 2x, partition data if growth exceeds 5TB. Cost projection: $12k/month current -> $35k/month projected. Optimization: spot instances for non-critical services, reserved instances for baseline capacity.

Postmortem: reporting data inconsistency incident. Date: 2026-05-15. Severity: CRITICAL. Duration: 3 hours. Impact: 5000 transactions with incorrect amounts, 2 hours of manual reconciliation. Summary: Dual-write to MongoDB and Kafka without transactional outbox caused partial writes — event published but database write failed. Root cause: code path did not wrap database write and event publish in a transaction. Detection: customer support ticket about incorrect account balance. Fix: implement transactional outbox pattern — write event to outbox table in same database transaction, separate process publishes events to Kafka. Prevention: (1) add architecture test enforcing outbox pattern for all event-publishing code paths, (2) add monitoring for outbox table lag, (3) add integration test verifying dual-write consistency under failure conditions. Blameless: root cause was junior engineer unaware of the pattern. Mitigation: added to onboarding checklist, documented in runbook, created template for event-publishing services.

Observability design: billing service. Metrics: RED (Rate, Error rate, Duration per endpoint). Rate: req/s by endpoint, status code, tenant. Error rate: % of 4xx and 5xx by endpoint. Duration: p50, p95, p99 latency. Resources: CPU, memory, GC pressure, connection pool utilization, database query latency. Logs: structured JSON with correlation_id, trace_id, span_id, service, version, environment. Log levels: ERROR (always sampled), WARN (always sampled), INFO (10% sampling), DEBUG (1% sampling). Traces: distributed tracing with OpenTelemetry, 100% sampling for errors, 1% sampling for all requests. Trace context: propagated via W3C traceparent header. Dashboards: service overview (RED + resources), dependencies (external call latency + error rate), business metrics (transactions per minute, active users, revenue impact). Alerts: P0 (error rate >5%, service down), P1 (p99 > 500ms, error rate >1%), P2 (CPU >80%, memory >80%).

Incident: onboarding service performance degradation. Severity: CRITICAL. Detection: PagerDuty alert fired — p99 latency exceeded 2s for 5 minutes (SLO: 200ms). Impact: 15% of users experiencing timeout errors on onboarding operations. Timeline: 14:02 alert fires, 14:05 engineer acknowledges, 14:12 identified root cause (database connection pool exhaustion due to deployment without proper warmup), 14:18 mitigation applied (restored previous connection pool config, restarted service), 14:25 all metrics green, 14:30 incident declared resolved. Root cause: deployment script did not pre-warm connection pool, causing 50 concurrent services to open connections simultaneously. Action items: [P0] add pre-warm step to deployment pipeline, [P1] increase max_connections with headroom, [P1] add connection pool utilization dashboard, [P2] implement gradual connection ramp-up in service startup.

Chaos experiment: feed database failover. Experiment type: planned failure of primary PostgreSQL instance. Hypothesis: application will failover to read replica within 30 seconds with <1% error rate. Blast radius: feed-api service only during low traffic window (02:00-04:00 UTC). Steady state: p99 latency < 200ms, error rate < 0.1%. Experiment steps: (1) inject latency on primary PostgreSQL connections (+500ms), (2) observe failover trigger, (3) hard fail primary instance, (4) measure time to failover completion. Results: failover completed in 18 seconds, 2.3% error rate during transition (higher than hypothesis). Analysis: connection timeout configured at 30s — too aggressive. Fix: reduce connection timeout to 5s with retry logic in C# client. Rerun experiment: failover in 12 seconds, 0.4% error rate. Hypothesis validated.

Traces: distributed tracing with OpenTelemetry, 100% sampling for errors, 1% sampling for all requests. Trace context: propagated via W3C traceparent header. Dashboards: service overview (RED + resources), dependencies (external call latency + error rate), business metrics (transactions per minute, active users, revenue impact). Alerts: P0 (error rate >5%, service down), P1 (p99 > 500ms, error rate >1%), P2 (CPU >80%, memory >80%).

Incident: backup service performance degradation. Severity: CRITICAL. Detection: PagerDuty alert fired — p99 latency exceeded 2s for 5 minutes (SLO: 200ms). Impact: 15% of users experiencing timeout errors on backup operations. Timeline: 14:02 alert fires, 14:05 engineer acknowledges, 14:12 identified root cause (database connection pool exhaustion due to deployment without proper warmup), 14:18 mitigation applied (restored previous connection pool config, restarted service), 14:25 all metrics green, 14:30 incident declared resolved. Root cause: deployment script did not pre-warm connection pool, causing 50 concurrent services to open connections simultaneously. Action items: [P0] add pre-warm step to deployment pipeline, [P1] increase max_connections with headroom, [P1] add connection pool utilization dashboard, [P2] implement gradual connection ramp-up in service startup.

Chaos experiment: scheduling database failover. Experiment type: planned failure of primary DynamoDB instance. Hypothesis: application will failover to read replica within 30 seconds with <1% error rate. Blast radius: scheduling-api service only during low traffic window (02:00-04:00 UTC). Steady state: p99 latency < 200ms, error rate < 0.1%. Experiment steps: (1) inject latency on primary DynamoDB connections (+500ms), (2) observe failover trigger, (3) hard fail primary instance, (4) measure time to failover completion. Results: failover completed in 18 seconds, 2.3% error rate during transition (higher than hypothesis). Analysis: connection timeout configured at 30s — too aggressive. Fix: reduce connection timeout to 5s with retry logic in C# client. Rerun experiment: failover in 12 seconds, 0.4% error rate. Hypothesis validated.

Toil elimination: workflow manual deployment process. Current process: engineer manually runs 15-step deployment checklist, monitors dashboards for 30 minutes post-deployment, handles rollback manually if issues detected. Frequency: 3 deploys/week. Time spent: 3 hours/deploy = 9 hours/week. Toil score: 3 (significant manual effort, no automation). Automated process: CI/CD pipeline with GitHub Actions + Fly.io CDK. Steps automated: (1) build and test in CI, (2) deploy to staging with smoke tests, (3) deploy to production with canary (5% -> 25% -> 100%), (4) automated canary analysis with metrics comparison, (5) automated rollback on metric regression. New time: 15 minutes review time per deploy. Toil saved: 8.25 hours/week. Toil score: 0.5 (minimal manual intervention). Next: automate dependency updates, automate database migration verification.

SLO: audit service availability SLO definition. Service: audit-api. SLI: proportion of successful HTTP requests (status < 500) measured over 1-minute windows. Target: 99.95% availability over 28-day rolling window. Error budget: 0.05% × 28 days = 20.16 minutes of allowable downtime. Burn rate alerting: page if burn rate exceeds 2x for 1 hour (consuming 8.33% of budget) or 10x for 6 minutes (consuming 4.17% of budget). Implementation: GCP CloudWatch / GCP Cloud Monitoring / Azure Monitor with MQL-based alerting. Multi-window, multi-burn-rate alerts: fast burn (10x, 5min window) and slow burn (2x, 1hr window).

Capacity plan: payment service for next 12 months. Current load: 2500 req/s peak, 800 req/s average, 150M req/month. Growth: 3x in 12 months based on business projections. Required capacity at peak: 7500 req/s. Current architecture: DigitalOcean ECS with 10 instances of Python service, each handling 250 req/s. Database: MySQL with 500 connections, 60% CPU at peak. Recommendation: scale to 30 instances (horizontal scaling), add read replicas for reporting workload, implement caching layer with Redis (target 90% cache hit ratio), upgrade database instance size by 2x, partition data if growth exceeds 5TB. Cost projection: $12k/month current -> $35k/month projected. Optimization: spot instances for non-critical services, reserved instances for baseline capacity.

Postmortem: inventory data inconsistency incident. Date: 2026-05-15. Severity: CRITICAL. Duration: 3 hours. Impact: 5000 transactions with incorrect amounts, 2 hours of manual reconciliation. Summary: Dual-write to Redis and Kafka without transactional outbox caused partial writes — event published but database write failed. Root cause: code path did not wrap database write and event publish in a transaction. Detection: customer support ticket about incorrect account balance. Fix: implement transactional outbox pattern — write event to outbox table in same database transaction, separate process publishes events to Kafka. Prevention: (1) add architecture test enforcing outbox pattern for all event-publishing code paths, (2) add monitoring for outbox table lag, (3) add integration test verifying dual-write consistency under failure conditions. Blameless: root cause was junior engineer unaware of the pattern. Mitigation: added to onboarding checklist, documented in runbook, created template for event-publishing services.

Burn rate alerting: page if burn rate exceeds 2x for 1 hour (consuming 8.33% of budget) or 10x for 6 minutes (consuming 4.17% of budget). Implementation: Fly.io CloudWatch / GCP Cloud Monitoring / Azure Monitor with MQL-based alerting. Multi-window, multi-burn-rate alerts: fast burn (10x, 5min window) and slow burn (2x, 1hr window).

Capacity plan: billing service for next 12 months. Current load: 2500 req/s peak, 800 req/s average, 150M req/month. Growth: 3x in 12 months based on business projections. Required capacity at peak: 7500 req/s. Current architecture: GCP ECS with 10 instances of Python service, each handling 250 req/s. Database: Redis with 500 connections, 60% CPU at peak. Recommendation: scale to 30 instances (horizontal scaling), add read replicas for reporting workload, implement caching layer with Redis (target 90% cache hit ratio), upgrade database instance size by 2x, partition data if growth exceeds 5TB. Cost projection: $12k/month current -> $35k/month projected. Optimization: spot instances for non-critical services, reserved instances for baseline capacity.

Postmortem: onboarding data inconsistency incident. Date: 2026-05-15. Severity: CRITICAL. Duration: 3 hours. Impact: 5000 transactions with incorrect amounts, 2 hours of manual reconciliation. Summary: Dual-write to Cassandra and Kafka without transactional outbox caused partial writes — event published but database write failed. Root cause: code path did not wrap database write and event publish in a transaction. Detection: customer support ticket about incorrect account balance. Fix: implement transactional outbox pattern — write event to outbox table in same database transaction, separate process publishes events to Kafka. Prevention: (1) add architecture test enforcing outbox pattern for all event-publishing code paths, (2) add monitoring for outbox table lag, (3) add integration test verifying dual-write consistency under failure conditions. Blameless: root cause was junior engineer unaware of the pattern. Mitigation: added to onboarding checklist, documented in runbook, created template for event-publishing services.

Observability design: feed service. Metrics: RED (Rate, Error rate, Duration per endpoint). Rate: req/s by endpoint, status code, tenant. Error rate: % of 4xx and 5xx by endpoint. Duration: p50, p95, p99 latency. Resources: CPU, memory, GC pressure, connection pool utilization, database query latency. Logs: structured JSON with correlation_id, trace_id, span_id, service, version, environment. Log levels: ERROR (always sampled), WARN (always sampled), INFO (10% sampling), DEBUG (1% sampling). Traces: distributed tracing with OpenTelemetry, 100% sampling for errors, 1% sampling for all requests. Trace context: propagated via W3C traceparent header. Dashboards: service overview (RED + resources), dependencies (external call latency + error rate), business metrics (transactions per minute, active users, revenue impact). Alerts: P0 (error rate >5%, service down), P1 (p99 > 500ms, error rate >1%), P2 (CPU >80%, memory >80%).

Incident: review service performance degradation. Severity: CRITICAL. Detection: PagerDuty alert fired — p99 latency exceeded 2s for 5 minutes (SLO: 200ms). Impact: 15% of users experiencing timeout errors on review operations. Timeline: 14:02 alert fires, 14:05 engineer acknowledges, 14:12 identified root cause (database connection pool exhaustion due to deployment without proper warmup), 14:18 mitigation applied (restored previous connection pool config, restarted service), 14:25 all metrics green, 14:30 incident declared resolved. Root cause: deployment script did not pre-warm connection pool, causing 50 concurrent services to open connections simultaneously. Action items: [P0] add pre-warm step to deployment pipeline, [P1] increase max_connections with headroom, [P1] add connection pool utilization dashboard, [P2] implement gradual connection ramp-up in service startup.

Chaos experiment: moderation database failover. Experiment type: planned failure of primary SQLite instance. Hypothesis: application will failover to read replica within 30 seconds with <1% error rate. Blast radius: moderation-api service only during low traffic window (02:00-04:00 UTC). Steady state: p99 latency < 200ms, error rate < 0.1%. Experiment steps: (1) inject latency on primary SQLite connections (+500ms), (2) observe failover trigger, (3) hard fail primary instance, (4) measure time to failover completion. Results: failover completed in 18 seconds, 2.3% error rate during transition (higher than hypothesis). Analysis: connection timeout configured at 30s — too aggressive. Fix: reduce connection timeout to 5s with retry logic in Kotlin client. Rerun experiment: failover in 12 seconds, 0.4% error rate. Hypothesis validated.

Toil elimination: export manual deployment process. Current process: engineer manually runs 15-step deployment checklist, monitors dashboards for 30 minutes post-deployment, handles rollback manually if issues detected. Frequency: 3 deploys/week. Time spent: 3 hours/deploy = 9 hours/week. Toil score: 3 (significant manual effort, no automation). Automated process: CI/CD pipeline with GitHub Actions + DigitalOcean CDK. Steps automated: (1) build and test in CI, (2) deploy to staging with smoke tests, (3) deploy to production with canary (5% -> 25% -> 100%), (4) automated canary analysis with metrics comparison, (5) automated rollback on metric regression. New time: 15 minutes review time per deploy. Toil saved: 8.25 hours/week. Toil score: 0.5 (minimal manual intervention). Next: automate dependency updates, automate database migration verification.

Timeline: 14:02 alert fires, 14:05 engineer acknowledges, 14:12 identified root cause (database connection pool exhaustion due to deployment without proper warmup), 14:18 mitigation applied (restored previous connection pool config, restarted service), 14:25 all metrics green, 14:30 incident declared resolved. Root cause: deployment script did not pre-warm connection pool, causing 50 concurrent services to open connections simultaneously. Action items: [P0] add pre-warm step to deployment pipeline, [P1] increase max_connections with headroom, [P1] add connection pool utilization dashboard, [P2] implement gradual connection ramp-up in service startup.

Chaos experiment: audit database failover. Experiment type: planned failure of primary Elasticsearch instance. Hypothesis: application will failover to read replica within 30 seconds with <1% error rate. Blast radius: audit-api service only during low traffic window (02:00-04:00 UTC). Steady state: p99 latency < 200ms, error rate < 0.1%. Experiment steps: (1) inject latency on primary Elasticsearch connections (+500ms), (2) observe failover trigger, (3) hard fail primary instance, (4) measure time to failover completion. Results: failover completed in 18 seconds, 2.3% error rate during transition (higher than hypothesis). Analysis: connection timeout configured at 30s — too aggressive. Fix: reduce connection timeout to 5s with retry logic in Kotlin client. Rerun experiment: failover in 12 seconds, 0.4% error rate. Hypothesis validated.

Toil elimination: payment manual deployment process. Current process: engineer manually runs 15-step deployment checklist, monitors dashboards for 30 minutes post-deployment, handles rollback manually if issues detected. Frequency: 3 deploys/week. Time spent: 3 hours/deploy = 9 hours/week. Toil score: 3 (significant manual effort, no automation). Automated process: CI/CD pipeline with GitHub Actions + GCP CDK. Steps automated: (1) build and test in CI, (2) deploy to staging with smoke tests, (3) deploy to production with canary (5% -> 25% -> 100%), (4) automated canary analysis with metrics comparison, (5) automated rollback on metric regression. New time: 15 minutes review time per deploy. Toil saved: 8.25 hours/week. Toil score: 0.5 (minimal manual intervention). Next: automate dependency updates, automate database migration verification.

SLO: inventory service availability SLO definition. Service: inventory-api. SLI: proportion of successful HTTP requests (status < 500) measured over 1-minute windows. Target: 99.95% availability over 28-day rolling window. Error budget: 0.05% × 28 days = 20.16 minutes of allowable downtime. Burn rate alerting: page if burn rate exceeds 2x for 1 hour (consuming 8.33% of budget) or 10x for 6 minutes (consuming 4.17% of budget). Implementation: DigitalOcean CloudWatch / GCP Cloud Monitoring / Azure Monitor with MQL-based alerting. Multi-window, multi-burn-rate alerts: fast burn (10x, 5min window) and slow burn (2x, 1hr window).

Capacity plan: user-profile service for next 12 months. Current load: 2500 req/s peak, 800 req/s average, 150M req/month. Growth: 3x in 12 months based on business projections. Required capacity at peak: 7500 req/s. Current architecture: Linode ECS with 10 instances of C# service, each handling 250 req/s. Database: CockroachDB with 500 connections, 60% CPU at peak. Recommendation: scale to 30 instances (horizontal scaling), add read replicas for reporting workload, implement caching layer with Redis (target 90% cache hit ratio), upgrade database instance size by 2x, partition data if growth exceeds 5TB. Cost projection: $12k/month current -> $35k/month projected. Optimization: spot instances for non-critical services, reserved instances for baseline capacity.

Postmortem: search data inconsistency incident. Date: 2026-05-15. Severity: CRITICAL. Duration: 3 hours. Impact: 5000 transactions with incorrect amounts, 2 hours of manual reconciliation. Summary: Dual-write to ClickHouse and Kafka without transactional outbox caused partial writes — event published but database write failed. Root cause: code path did not wrap database write and event publish in a transaction. Detection: customer support ticket about incorrect account balance. Fix: implement transactional outbox pattern — write event to outbox table in same database transaction, separate process publishes events to Kafka. Prevention: (1) add architecture test enforcing outbox pattern for all event-publishing code paths, (2) add monitoring for outbox table lag, (3) add integration test verifying dual-write consistency under failure conditions. Blameless: root cause was junior engineer unaware of the pattern. Mitigation: added to onboarding checklist, documented in runbook, created template for event-publishing services.

Observability design: reporting service. Metrics: RED (Rate, Error rate, Duration per endpoint). Rate: req/s by endpoint, status code, tenant. Error rate: % of 4xx and 5xx by endpoint. Duration: p50, p95, p99 latency. Resources: CPU, memory, GC pressure, connection pool utilization, database query latency. Logs: structured JSON with correlation_id, trace_id, span_id, service, version, environment. Log levels: ERROR (always sampled), WARN (always sampled), INFO (10% sampling), DEBUG (1% sampling). Traces: distributed tracing with OpenTelemetry, 100% sampling for errors, 1% sampling for all requests. Trace context: propagated via W3C traceparent header. Dashboards: service overview (RED + resources), dependencies (external call latency + error rate), business metrics (transactions per minute, active users, revenue impact). Alerts: P0 (error rate >5%, service down), P1 (p99 > 500ms, error rate >1%), P2 (CPU >80%, memory >80%).

Incident: payment DB (MySQL) CPU spike. Severity: CRITICAL. Detection: PagerDuty alert — DB CPU >90% for 5min. Impact: p99 latency 2s+, 15% timeout errors. Timeline: 14:02 alert, 14:05 acknowledge, 14:12 root cause identified (missing index causing sequential scan on 50M row table), 14:18 mitigation (CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY), 14:25 metrics green, 14:30 resolved. Root cause: deployment added new query without index review. Actions: [P0] add EXPLAIN ANALYZE to CI pipeline, [P1] index review in PR template, [P1] DB CPU dashboard with per-query breakdown. Blameless: process gap in deployment pipeline, not individual error.

Root cause: deployment added new query without index review. Actions: [P0] add EXPLAIN ANALYZE to CI pipeline, [P1] index review in PR template, [P1] DB CPU dashboard with per-query breakdown. Blameless: process gap in deployment pipeline, not individual error.

Capacity: payment Python on Hetzner. Current: 2500 req/s peak, 800 avg, 150M/mo. Growth: 3x in 12mo. Required: 7500 req/s peak. Architecture: GCP with 10 instances (250 req/s each). DB: DynamoDB 500 connections, 60% CPU. Plan: scale to 30 instances horizontally, add read replicas for reporting, Redis cache (90% hit ratio), upgrade DB 2x, partition if >5TB. Cost: $12k/mo -> $35k/mo. Optimization: spot instances for batch, reserved for baseline, rightsize after 90d monitoring. Validation: load test at 2x peak before procurement.

Chaos: payment Redis failover experiment. Hypothesis: failover to replica within 30s with <1% error rate. Blast radius: payment service during 02:00-04:00 UTC. Steady state: p99 < 200ms, error < 0.1%. Steps: (1) inject +500ms latency on Redis, (2) fail primary, (3) measure failover time. Result: failover 18s, 2.3% error rate. Analysis: connection timeout 30s too aggressive. Fix: timeout 5s with Python retry logic. Rerun: failover 12s, 0.4% error. Hypothesis validated. Next experiment: admin cache node failure, multi-region failover test.

Fix: timeout 5s with Python retry logic. Rerun: failover 12s, 0.4% error. Hypothesis validated. Next experiment: queue cache node failure, multi-region failover test.

Postmortem: payment data inconsistency on SQLite via Rust. Severity: CRITICAL. Duration: 3hr. Impact: 5000 transactions with incorrect amounts, 2hr manual reconciliation. Summary: dual-write to SQLite + Kafka without outbox — event published but DB write failed. Fix: transactional outbox — write event to outbox in same DB transaction, Debezium CDC publishes to Kafka. Prevention: (1) architecture test enforcing outbox for all event-publishing code, (2) outbox lag monitoring, (3) integration test for dual-write consistency under failure. Action: add to onboarding checklist, document in runbook, template for event-publishing services.

Toil: payment manual deployment on DigitalOcean. Current: 15-step manual checklist, 30min post-deploy monitoring, manual rollback. 3 deploys/week, 3hr each = 9hr/week. Toil score: 3 (significant manual effort). Automated: GitHub Actions + DigitalOcean CDK. Build -> test -> staging deploy with smoke tests -> canary (5%/25%/100%) -> automated analysis -> auto-rollback on regression. New time: 15min review. Toil saved: 8.25hr/week. Toil score: 0.5. Next: automate dependency updates (Dependabot), database migration verification in CI, post-deploy health validation with automated runbook.

Observability: payment on OVH. Metrics: RED (Rate, Error, Duration per endpoint) + resources (CPU, memory, GC, connections). Logs: structured JSON with correlation_id, trace_id, span_id, service, version. ERROR always, WARN always, INFO 10%, DEBUG 1%. Traces: OpenTelemetry, 100% error sampling, 1% all requests, W3C traceparent propagation. Dashboards: service overview (RED + resources), dependencies (external call latency + error rate), business (transactions/min, active users). Alerts: P0 (error >5%, service down), P1 (p99 >500ms, error >1%), P2 (CPU >80%, memory >80%). Runbooks: documented for every P0/P1 alert with investigation steps.

Traces: OpenTelemetry, 100% error sampling, 1% all requests, W3C traceparent propagation. Dashboards: service overview (RED + resources), dependencies (external call latency + error rate), business (transactions/min, active users). Alerts: P0 (error >5%, service down), P1 (p99 >500ms, error >1%), P2 (CPU >80%, memory >80%). Runbooks: documented for every P0/P1 alert with investigation steps.

Traces: OpenTelemetry, 100% error sampling, 1% all requests, W3C traceparent propagation. Dashboards: service overview (RED + resources), dependencies (external call latency + error rate), business (transactions/min, active users). Alerts: P0 (error >5%, service down), P1 (p99 >500ms, error >1%), P2 (CPU >80%, memory >80%). Runbooks: documented for every P0/P1 alert with investigation steps.

Traces: OpenTelemetry, 100% error sampling, 1% all requests, W3C traceparent propagation. Dashboards: service overview (RED + resources), dependencies (external call latency + error rate), business (transactions/min, active users). Alerts: P0 (error >5%, service down), P1 (p99 >500ms, error >1%), P2 (CPU >80%, memory >80%). Runbooks: documented for every P0/P1 alert with investigation steps.

Traces: OpenTelemetry, 100% error sampling, 1% all requests, W3C traceparent propagation. Dashboards: service overview (RED + resources), dependencies (external call latency + error rate), business (transactions/min, active users). Alerts: P0 (error >5%, service down), P1 (p99 >500ms, error >1%), P2 (CPU >80%, memory >80%). Runbooks: documented for every P0/P1 alert with investigation steps.

Traces: OpenTelemetry, 100% error sampling, 1% all requests, W3C traceparent propagation. Dashboards: service overview (RED + resources), dependencies (external call latency + error rate), business (transactions/min, active users). Alerts: P0 (error >5%, service down), P1 (p99 >500ms, error >1%), P2 (CPU >80%, memory >80%). Runbooks: documented for every P0/P1 alert with investigation steps.

Traces: OpenTelemetry, 100% error sampling, 1% all requests, W3C traceparent propagation. Dashboards: service overview (RED + resources), dependencies (external call latency + error rate), business (transactions/min, active users). Alerts: P0 (error >5%, service down), P1 (p99 >500ms, error >1%), P2 (CPU >80%, memory >80%). Runbooks: documented for every P0/P1 alert with investigation steps.

Release: payment release engineering on Linode. Versioning: semver, git tag triggers CI. CI pipeline: lint -> type-check -> unit test (5min) -> build (3min) -> integration test (10min) -> security scan (5min) -> SBOM generation. CD: deploy staging (2min) -> smoke tests (3min) -> canary deploy 5% (5min) -> analysis -> 25% (5min) -> 50% (5min) -> 100% (5min). Total: ~45min from merge to production. Auto-rollback: revert to previous version if error rate >1% increase within 30min. Gate: manual approval for production deploy on Friday afternoons (change freeze window).

CD: deploy staging (2min) -> smoke tests (3min) -> canary deploy 5% (5min) -> analysis -> 25% (5min) -> 50% (5min) -> 100% (5min). Total: ~45min from merge to production. Auto-rollback: revert to previous version if error rate >1% increase within 30min. Gate: manual approval for production deploy on Friday afternoons (change freeze window).

Alert: payment latency-degradation. Severity: P1. Symptoms: error rate >5%, p99 latency >2s. Investigation: (1) check deploy dashboard for recent changes, (2) check dependency health for cascading failures, (3) check logs for error pattern. Runbook: latency-degradation.md versioned in ops repo. Mitigation: (1) rollback recent deploy if cause identified, (2) increase resource limits temporarily, (3) redirect traffic to healthy region. Escalation: team lead if not resolved in 15min, EM in 30min, VP Eng in 1hr. Post-incident: timeline documented, root cause analysis within 48hr, action items tracked in backlog with P0 priority.

DR: payment disaster recovery on Hetzner. RPO: 5min for critical data via synchronous replication. RTO: 15min with auto-failover. Strategy: active-active multi-region (Hetzner region A + region B). Data: MySQL cross-region streaming replication. DNS: global traffic manager with health probe. Failover procedure: (1) health check failure in primary region triggers failover, (2) DNS updates to route traffic to secondary, (3) DB replica promoted to primary, (4) services scaled up in secondary. Test: quarterly DR exercise with full failover, validate RPO/RTO, document gaps. Last test: 28s RTO, 3s RPO — within targets.

Perf: payment C# load test on DigitalOcean. Test type: spike test (0 -> 10x in 30s). Baseline: 500 req/s, p99 150ms, error rate 0.1%. Spike: 5000 req/s — p99 climbs to 2.8s, error rate 8%. Bottleneck: MySQL connection pool exhaustion at 200 concurrent connections. Fix: increase pool to 500, add PgBouncer connection pooling, implement response caching with Redis. Retest: spike at 5000 req/s — p99 180ms, error rate 0.2%. DigitalOcean auto-scaling: triggered at 70% CPU, 3 additional instances provisioned within 90s. Recommendation: monthly load test, weekly perf regression check in CI.

Retest: spike at 5000 req/s — p99 180ms, error rate 0.2%. DigitalOcean auto-scaling: triggered at 70% CPU, 3 additional instances provisioned within 90s. Recommendation: monthly load test, weekly perf regression check in CI.

Retest: spike at 5000 req/s — p99 180ms, error rate 0.2%. Railway auto-scaling: triggered at 70% CPU, 3 additional instances provisioned within 90s. Recommendation: monthly load test, weekly perf regression check in CI.

Retest: spike at 5000 req/s — p99 180ms, error rate 0.2%. OVH auto-scaling: triggered at 70% CPU, 3 additional instances provisioned within 90s. Recommendation: monthly load test, weekly perf regression check in CI.

Retest: spike at 5000 req/s — p99 180ms, error rate 0.2%. GCP auto-scaling: triggered at 70% CPU, 3 additional instances provisioned within 90s. Recommendation: monthly load test, weekly perf regression check in CI.

Dependency: payment dependency management on Linode. Critical dependencies: GraphQL API, Hetzner S3, DynamoDB DB, Redis cache, Kafka event bus. Monitoring: per-dependency RED metrics dashboard. Health: Linode service health checks every 15s from each service instance. Circuit breaker: 5 consecutive failures -> open for 60s, half-open after 30s. Degraded mode: cached responses for API, local queue for Kafka, read-only for DB. Deprecation: 6-month migration window for GraphQL API version upgrades, tested in staging before production cutover.


Dependency: inventory dependency management on Fly.io. Critical dependencies: WebSocket API, Linode S3, SQLite DB, Redis cache, Kafka event bus. Monitoring: per-dependency RED metrics dashboard. Health: Fly.io service health checks every 15s from each service instance. Circuit breaker: 5 consecutive failures -> open for 60s, half-open after 30s. Degraded mode: cached responses for API, local queue for Kafka, read-only for DB. Deprecation: 6-month migration window for WebSocket API version upgrades, tested in staging before production cutover.

Degraded mode: cached responses for API, local queue for Kafka, read-only for DB. Deprecation: 6-month migration window for GraphQL API version upgrades, tested in staging before production cutover.

Degraded mode: cached responses for API, local queue for Kafka, read-only for DB. Deprecation: 6-month migration window for Webhook API version upgrades, tested in staging before production cutover.

Degraded mode: cached responses for API, local queue for Kafka, read-only for DB. Deprecation: 6-month migration window for AMQP API version upgrades, tested in staging before production cutover.

Degraded mode: cached responses for API, local queue for Kafka, read-only for DB. Deprecation: 6-month migration window for WebSocket API version upgrades, tested in staging before production cutover.

Oncall: payment oncall operations. Rotation: 1 week primary + 1 week secondary, 8 engineers, 8-week cycle. Hours: P0/P1 24/7 follow-the-sun, P2 business hours. Handover: 30min overlap, review active incidents, unresolved tickets, upcoming changes. Incident management: (1) acknowledge within 5min, (2) assess severity within 10min, (3) mitigate within 30min for P0, 1hr for P1. Escalation: primary -> secondary -> team lead -> EM -> VP Eng. Post-incident: timeline documentation within 24hr, root cause analysis within 48hr. Quality of life: automated runbooks for common incidents, no oncall tasks during non-incident time, oncall compensation / rotation credit.

Post-incident: timeline documentation within 24hr, root cause analysis within 48hr. Quality of life: automated runbooks for common incidents, no oncall tasks during non-incident time, oncall compensation / rotation credit.

Reliability: payment reliability testing on GCP. Types: (1) unit test for error handling paths (100% coverage of catch blocks), (2) integration test with dependency failure scenarios (WireMock for each dependency), (3) chaos experiment for infrastructure failures (pod kill, network latency, disk pressure), (4) load test at 1x/2x/5x peak traffic, (5) Soak test for 24hr at 1x traffic to detect memory leaks, (6) failover test for DB/cache/message broker. Cadence: (1)-(3) in every release, (4)-(5) monthly, (6) quarterly. Gate: all reliability tests must pass before production deployment. Dashboard: reliability score trending over time.

Cadence: (1)-(3) in every release, (4)-(5) monthly, (6) quarterly. Gate: all reliability tests must pass before production deployment. Dashboard: reliability score trending over time.

Cost: payment OVH cost optimization. Compute: 30% underutilized — right-size with 90d metric analysis, switch batch workloads to spot (60% savings), reserved instances for baseline (40% discount). Storage: move cold data to S3 Glacier (70% savings), enable lifecycle policies. Network: compress API responses, enable OVH CDN for static content, use private IP for inter-service communication. DB: MySQL read replicas for reporting, auto-scaling, reserved capacity. Savings: $12k/mo -> $8.5k/mo (29% reduction). Storage: move cold data to S3 Glacier (70% savings), enable lifecycle policies. Network: compress API responses, enable DigitalOcean CDN for static content, use private IP for inter-service communication. DB: ClickHouse read replicas for reporting, auto-scaling, reserved capacity. Savings: $12k/mo -> $8.5k/mo (29% reduction). Monitor: cost per service per environment, budget alerts at 80%/100%, weekly cost review.
